entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8077"/><div sID="gen12558" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8077"/>3. Even if a man (of this character) have very many (equivalent to "a hundred," <reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.1">2Ki 10:1</reference>) children, and not have a "stranger" as his heir (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.2">Ec 6:2</reference>), and live long ("days of years" express the brevity of life at its best, <reference osisRef="Gen.47.9">Ge 47:9</reference>), yet enjoy no real "good" in life, and lie unhonored, without "burial," at death (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.26">2Ki 9:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.35">35</reference>), the embryo is better than he. In the East to be without burial is the greatest degradation. "Better the fruit that drops from the tree before it is ripe than that left to hang on till rotten" [Henry]. <div eID="gen12558" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8080"/><div sID="gen12563" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8080"/>6. If the miser's length of "life" be thought to raise him above the abortive, Solomon answers that long life, without enjoying real good, is but lengthened misery, and riches cannot exempt him from going whither "all go." He is fit neither for life, nor death, nor eternity. <div eID="gen12563" type="x-p"/>

This is the advantage:<div eID="gen12569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12570" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Better is the sight of the eyes--</hi>the wise man's godly enjoyment of present seen blessings<div eID="gen12570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12571" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">than the (fool's) wandering--</hi>literally, walking (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.9">Psa 73:9</reference>), of the desire, that is, vague, insatiable desires for what he has not (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.7">Ec 6:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.5">He 13:5</reference>).<div eID="gen12571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12572" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this--</hi>restless wandering of desire, and not enjoying contentedly the present (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.6">1Ti 6:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.8">8</reference>). <div eID="gen12572" type="x-p"/>

Since man's toils are vain, what is the chief good? (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.12">Ec 6:12</reference>). The answer is contained in the rest of the book.<div eID="gen12573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12574" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">That which hath been--</hi>man's various circumstances<div eID="gen12574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12575" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is named already--</hi>not only has existed, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.9">Ec 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.15">3:15</reference>, but has received its just name, "vanity," long ago,<div eID="gen12575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12576" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and it is known that it--</hi>vanity<div eID="gen12576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12577" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is man--</hi>Hebrew, "Adam," equivalent to man "of red dust," as his Creator appropriately named him from his frailty.<div eID="gen12577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12578" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither may he contend, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rom.9.20">Ro 9:20</reference>). <div eID="gen12578" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 10. Part II begins here. Since man's toils are vain, what is the chief good? ( Ec 6:12 ). The answer is contained in the rest of the book. That which hath been-- man's various circumstances is named already-- not only has existed, Ec 1:9 ; 3:15 , but has received its just name, "vanity," long ago, and it is known that it-- vanity is man-- Hebrew, "Adam," equivalent to man "of red dust," as his Creator appropriately named him from his frailty. neither may he contend, &c.-- ( Ro 9:20 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8086"/><div sID="gen12581" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8086"/><hi type="bold">12. For who knoweth, &c.--</hi>The ungodly know not what is really "good" during life, nor "what shall be after them," that is, what will be the event of their undertakings (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.22">Ec 3:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.7">8:7</reference>). The godly might be tempted to "contend with God" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.10">Ec 6:10</reference>) as to His dispensations; but they cannot fully know the wise purposes served by them now and hereafter. Their sufferings from the oppressors are more really good for them than cloudless prosperity; sinners are being allowed to fill up their measure of guilt. Retribution in part vindicates God's ways even now. The judgment shall make all clear. In <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.1-Eccl.7.29">Ec 7:1-29</reference>, he states what is good, in answer to this verse. <chapter eID="Eccl.6"/>
